teaser: A rescue that fails: the saint asks to stay on the cross, and nobody can untie him.
review_notes:
Patron: Juan Alfonso Pimentel de Herrera, Count of Benavente, viceroy of Naples 1603-1610; he took the painting to Valladolid in 1610 (standard account).
Benavente's sponsorship of the renovation of the crypt of Saint Andrew at Amalfi: fairly sure, please check.
The figure of 20,000 people comes from the Golden Legend.
Identification of the armored man as the proconsul Aegeas is the usual reading, not certain.
Cleveland acquired the painting in 1976; public conservation 2014-2016 and display next to the so-called Back-Vega version in 2017: please check dates.
Size about 202.5 x 152.7 cm.

lesson.text: The first person to live with this painting could not bear to leave it behind. He was the Count of Benavente, who ruled Naples for the king of Spain. When his term ended in 1610, he had the canvas, two meters tall (about 6 ft 8 in), packed and shipped home to his palace in Valladolid. Painters who had seen it in Naples went on making copies.

He had ordered it around 1607 from the most talked-about painter in Italy, who was also a wanted man. A year earlier, Caravaggio had killed an opponent in a street fight in Rome and fled south with a death sentence on his head. Naples, under Spanish rule, was out of the pope's reach. Commissions poured in.

The story is stranger than a simple execution. Andrew, one of the twelve apostles, is tied to a cross in the Greek city of Patras. He hangs there for two days, preaching to a crowd that the old legend puts at 20,000 people. They turn on the governor and demand that Andrew be freed. The governor gives in. Andrew does not want to come down.

He prays to be allowed to die on the cross as his master did. At that instant, says the legend, the arms of the men sent to untie him go limp and useless. Caravaggio has to paint something nearly impossible: a man working with all his strength and getting nowhere.
A man has climbed a ladder to set Andrew free. Tap the knot he is struggling with.

spots.title: The rope that will not give
spots.text: Top left corner: thick cord wound around the saint's wrist and the beam. The executioner's two fists are locked on it. Seen from behind, his whole back strains, and nothing moves.

lesson.text: Follow that man down from his fists. His shoulders twist, his white shirt has slipped off, his yellow breeches bunch at the knee, and his bare foot grips a rung at the very bottom of the canvas. He fills the left half of the picture with effort. And yet the knot holds. The miracle is shown as a job that cannot be done.

Andrew is usually shown on an X-shaped cross, the one that became the white diagonal on the flag of Scotland. That image only became standard later. Caravaggio followed the older tradition of an upright cross, and tied his saint with ropes instead of nails, as the legend says.

Nearly everything else is darkness. Caravaggio's method, later called tenebrism, means lighting a few bodies hard against a black ground, as if a shutter had been opened in a cellar. There is no landscape, no city of Patras, no sky. The light picks out only what the story needs.

lesson.title: The body on the cross
lesson.text: The light falls from the upper left and runs down the saint from head to feet.

spots.title: The last breath
spots.text: The head rolls to one side, mouth open, eyes half closed and turned upward. Gray beard, sunburnt forehead, deep creases. This is an old laborer's face, painted from a real model.

spots.title: The chest
spots.text: Ribs, sagging skin and a hollow belly, lit almost cruelly. The face and neck are tanned, the torso pale: the body of a man who worked outdoors with his shirt on.

spots.title: The feet
spots.text: They are tied with cord at the ankles and hang among the onlookers, toenails catching the light. Caravaggio puts them close to us, at the height of the crowd's faces.

lesson.text: That tanned neck above a white chest tells you how Caravaggio worked. He did not invent an ideal saint from old statues. He posed a living old man in his studio and painted what was in front of him, sunburn included. In 1607 this honesty shocked some viewers and thrilled others.

Down in the shadows stand the people who came to watch. There are only four of them, standing for a crowd of thousands, and each one reacts differently. Look at them one by one, because Caravaggio gives each of them a question of their own.

spots.title: The old woman
spots.text: She looks up from the foot of the ladder, face lined and attentive. Under her chin swells a goiter, a lump on the neck caused by a thyroid illness. She is the picture's believer.

spots.title: The man in the hat
spots.text: Seen from behind, head tipped back, bearded cheek in the light. He is usually read as Aegeas, the governor who ordered the execution and now cannot undo it.

spots.title: Armor
spots.text: A steel sleeve with a few streaks of white paint for the gleam. It is the only cold, hard surface in a painting made of skin and cloth.

spots.title: The open mouth
spots.text: Between the armor and the cross, a face in shadow gapes upward. You can almost hear him. He has understood that something is wrong.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: On the right, the second wrist is bound with the same rope, fingers curling. This side of the cross sinks into darkness and smoky cloud.

spots.title: The red cloth
spots.text: A strip of red knotted at the hips, the only strong color near the saint. Beside it hangs the executioner's yellow. Two colors, two men, back to back.

lesson.text: A goiter comes from a lack of iodine in the diet and used to be common in poor inland and mountain regions. By painting it, Caravaggio marks the woman as a peasant from the countryside around Naples, the kind of person altar paintings usually left out.

Notice what is missing. No angel arrives with a martyr's crown, no heaven opens. The only sign of the miracle is a rope that stays tied and a dying man's upward look. Caravaggio asks you to believe the story on the evidence of bodies alone.
Caravaggio turns a miracle into something you could witness: real people, one hard light, and the exact second between living and dying.

The canvas dropped out of sight in Spain for centuries and was bought by the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1976. When it needed cleaning, the museum did the work in a gallery, in front of visitors, so the public could watch dark old varnish come off inch by inch.

Go back to the man in armor. From where he stands he sees the bound feet, the red cloth, the chin from below. He has power over everyone in this picture and it has just stopped working. Caravaggio does not show his face in full, so what he feels is left for you to decide.

quiz.question: What is the man on the ladder trying to do?
quiz.explanation: He was sent to free the saint, but his arms fail him.

quiz.question: Who first owned the painting?
quiz.explanation: The Count of Benavente ordered it and took it to Spain in 1610.

quiz.question: What does tenebrism mean?
options: Lighting figures strongly against a dark background
quiz.explanation: A few bodies are lit hard while the rest stays black.

quiz.question: What does the old woman have on her neck?
quiz.explanation: The swelling is a goiter, a thyroid condition common among the poor.

quiz.question: Why was Caravaggio in Naples?
options: He had fled Rome after killing a man
He was the viceroy's court painter since childhood
quiz.explanation: He ran south after a deadly street fight in Rome.

quiz.question: What kind of cross does Caravaggio paint?
options: A cross lying on the ground
An upright cross with ropes instead of nails
quiz.explanation: He follows the older tradition of an upright cross.

facts.text: In the legend, Andrew begs to be taken down from the cross.
facts.explanation: He asks to stay and die there; the crowd is the one demanding his release.

facts.text: An angel with a crown appears at the top of the painting.
facts.explanation: There is no angel and no opening sky, only darkness.

facts.text: The saint's face and neck are more tanned than his chest.
facts.explanation: Caravaggio painted a real model, sunburn and all.
